title: WAS THAT GOD… OR WAS THAT JUST ME?
paragraphs:
WAS THAT GOD… OR WAS THAT JUST ME?
How to Distinguish God’s Voice From Your Own When Your Heart Is Loud, Your Emotions Are Real, and You’re Terrified of Getting It Wrong
There is a frightening sentence Christians sometimes say with absolute confidence:
Sometimes it leads to obedience, humility, repentance, reconciliation, courage, generosity, forgiveness, and deeper dependence on Jesus Christ.
That possibility should humble every one of us.
Because one of the most dangerous spiritual mistakes is not simply refusing to listen to God.
It is putting God’s name on something He never said.
You prayed about the opportunity that suddenly appeared.
Someone said something that seemed almost too perfectly timed.
And now you are sitting there wondering…
Or perhaps the question underneath the question is even more painful:
“What if I desperately want this to be God because I desperately want this?”
That is where discernment becomes uncomfortable.
Because sometimes the voice we are most likely to mistake for God is our own voice after we have baptized our desires in spiritual language.
We can even call disobedience “God leading me in a different direction.”
And if you have ever made a decision believing God was leading you, only to watch everything collapse afterward, you know how deeply this question can wound the soul.
Was I hearing myself the entire time?
Can I ever trust spiritual guidance again?
Here is where we need something stronger than feelings.
Not because God is distant, but because God has graciously given His people an objective standard by which subjective impressions can be tested.
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.”
τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἐμὰ τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούουσιν
ta probata ta ema tēs phōnēs mou akouousin
The verb ἀκούω — akouō means to hear or listen.
But we must be careful here.
John 10 is not primarily giving Christians a technique for identifying private inner messages about whom to marry, which career to choose, or whether to move to another city.
Jesus is describing Himself as the true Shepherd whose sheep recognize and follow Him, in contrast with thieves, strangers, and false shepherds.
The center of the passage is not our ability to decode mysterious impressions.
The Christian life is not primarily about becoming skilled at hearing whispers.
It is about becoming so anchored in the Shepherd revealed in Scripture that voices contrary to Him become increasingly recognizable.
If an impression tells you to hate someone, you do not need three confirmations.
If an impression tells you adultery is acceptable because “this person understands me better than my spouse,” you do not need another sign.
If something inside you says revenge will finally heal you, Scripture has already exposed the lie.

If a spiritual experience encourages pride, deception, greed, sexual immorality, bitterness, cruelty, idolatry, or rebellion against what God has clearly revealed, you do not need to ask whether God might be making an exception for you.
That sounds simple until your emotions become involved.
Because there are moments when what we want feels so powerful that we begin searching Scripture not to be corrected…
“Can I find something that sounds like permission?”
That is a very different posture.
And Scripture knows how deceptive the human interior can become.
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?”
The heart is profoundly deceptive, crooked, difficult to fully understand.
That does not mean every emotion is sinful.
It does not mean Christians should become suspicious of every desire.
It means your feelings are real without necessarily being reliable interpreters of God’s will.
Your feelings can be real without being revelation.
You can sincerely feel something and sincerely be wrong.
You can feel peace about something foolish.
You can feel terrified about something obedient.
You can feel excited about temptation.
You can feel uncomfortable while God is exposing your sin.
That is why “I feel peace about it” cannot become the final test of whether something came from God.
Obedience did not feel emotionally comfortable.
“Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.”
That sentence destroys one of modern Christianity’s most seductive assumptions:
that God's will will always feel peaceful.
Sometimes obedience requires ending something you desperately wanted to keep.
Sometimes obedience means confessing what you hoped nobody would ever discover.
Sometimes obedience means forgiving someone before your emotions have caught up with your decision.
Sometimes obedience means staying faithful when every selfish instinct tells you to run.
But peace is not permission to ignore Scripture.
And this is where discernment becomes deeply personal.
Maybe you have been asking God whether you should continue something He has already told you to surrender.
Maybe you are waiting for “confirmation” because obedience would hurt.
Maybe the reason heaven seems silent is not because God has failed to speak.
Maybe Scripture has already answered the question you keep asking.
Because sometimes we do not need another word from God.
We need courage to obey the Word He has already given.
δοκιμάζω — dokimazō carries the sense of examining, testing, or proving something in order to determine its genuineness.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
That means discernment is not unbelief.
And John immediately makes the test Christ-centered.
“Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God.”
Christian discernment therefore cannot be separated from Jesus Christ.
Ask what your supposed guidance does with Jesus.
or give sophisticated excuses for sin?
or make you feel spiritually superior because “God speaks to me differently”?
Does it draw you toward truth…
Does it make you more forgiving…
or give you religious vocabulary for resentment?
or merely toward what you already wanted?
Those questions can expose things that goosebumps cannot.
The Greek word translated “breathed out by God” is extraordinary:
Christians may debate how God guides believers in particular circumstances, but we should never place our private impressions on the same level as God-breathed Scripture.
Your pastor’s impression is not Scripture.
A prophetic claim is not Scripture.
A viral Christian video is not Scripture.
Everything must bow before what God has actually revealed.
Because it means you do not have to spend your entire Christian life terrified that one missed feeling will destroy God’s plan for you.
You have the wisdom of mature believers.
And above all, you have Jesus Christ.
God's guidance is not an escape room where one wrong clue ruins your destiny.
There are moral commands Scripture makes unmistakably clear, and there are wisdom decisions where several options may be permissible.
“Should I take the job in Manila or stay where I am?”
“Should I buy this house or that one?”
Those questions may not have a verse containing your personalized answer.
In those situations, biblical discernment may look less like waiting for an audible sentence and more like becoming wise.
You search Scripture for relevant principles.
You look at providential circumstances without treating every coincidence as a divine code.
You ask whether the decision allows you to honor Christ.
you make the wisest decision you can.
James gives us a beautiful promise:
“If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God…”
Sometimes we keep begging God for a sign while He is teaching us wisdom.
God may instead be forming a person capable of making faithful decisions behind either permissible door.
That kind of maturity is less dramatic.
And yes, Christians should pray for the Holy Spirit’s guidance.
“For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.”
Romans 8 is saturated with life in the Spirit, putting sin to death, belonging to Christ, adoption, suffering, hope, prayer, and conformity to Christ.
Being “led by the Spirit” cannot legitimately mean being led away from the character and commands of Christ.
That gives us another powerful question:
Does this make Jesus more precious to me, or does it simply make my desires feel more sacred?
There is another test that many people avoid because it requires community.
“The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but a wise man listens to advice.”
Sometimes what you call “God told me” needs to survive a conversation with spiritually mature believers who are not emotionally invested in getting the answer you want.
Not people who pretend to run your life.
Not someone whose authority replaces Scripture.
Wise, mature, Christ-centered believers who know God's Word and love you enough to disagree with you.
If you become furious whenever someone questions what you claim God told you, examine that reaction.
You might still ultimately disagree with someone's advice.
But if nobody is allowed to question your “word from God,” you have created a dangerous spiritual immunity around your own desires.
And perhaps this is where the deepest wound is hiding.
Because maybe you are reading this after getting it wrong.
You really believed God wanted the relationship.
You thought the opportunity was His will.
A mistaken impression does not put you beyond the mercy of Jesus.
The disciples misunderstood the nature of Christ's kingdom.
And Jesus did not throw Peter away.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him.
Christianity is not the story of spiritually gifted people becoming flawless at reading divine signals.
It is the story of sinners being rescued by the crucified and risen Son of God.
He took the judgment we deserved.
And sinners who repent and trust in Him receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
That means the ultimate question is bigger than:
Because you can spend years chasing supernatural experiences and still avoid surrender.
You can collect prophetic words and still refuse repentance.
You can memorize Christian language and still hide secret sin.
You can say “God told me” fifty times a week and rarely open the Bible.
But Jesus does not merely want to become another voice competing inside your head.
Maybe what you need tonight is not another sign.
Maybe there is something you already know must go.
The relationship pulling you away from Christ.
The religious performance covering spiritual emptiness.
You have been asking God to speak.
But perhaps His written Word has been sitting unopened beside you.
Not randomly hunting for a sentence that confirms what you want.
Because familiarity with God's Word trains discernment.
And when an impression comes, hold it with humility.

“Lord, I think this may be Your leading, but I could be wrong. Search my motives. Correct me through Your Word. Give me wisdom. Bring mature counsel. Close what should be closed. Give me courage to obey what You have clearly commanded. Above everything else, make me faithful to Jesus.”
There is tremendous freedom in praying like that.
You do not have to pretend certainty you do not possess.
Sometimes the most spiritually mature sentence you can say is:
“I believe God may be leading me this way, but I am testing it carefully.”
And if God has clearly spoken in Scripture, stop negotiating.
Not because obedience purchases His love.
We obey because salvation is grace, because Christ is Lord, and because those who love Him desire to keep His commands.
If this article exposed something you have been calling “God’s voice” that may actually be fear, desire, pride, loneliness, lust, anger, or desperation, do not hide from Jesus.
Someone reading silently may desperately need to know that failure was not the final chapter.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelievers to follow too—not because a page can save anybody, but because people desperately need to keep encountering Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Not because giving money proves that you love Jesus.
And never because God's grace can be purchased.

But if you genuinely want another practical way to glorify God, one way you can do that is by voluntarily supporting and sharing faithful Gospel work so that biblical teaching can continue reaching people who desperately need Jesus.
Because somewhere behind a smiling profile picture may be a believer terrified that God has stopped speaking.
Somewhere is a woman about to mistake loneliness for confirmation.
Somewhere is a man about to call temptation “peace.”
Somewhere is a wounded Christian who made the wrong decision years ago and still believes God wants nothing to do with them.
And somewhere is a person who does not merely need direction.
“Does this produce obedience rather than excuse sin?”
“Am I willing for Your answer to be different from what I want?”
“Can mature believers examine this with me?”
“Jesus, if You take away everything I wanted, will I still want You?”
There is the heart of discernment.
Not chasing signs until God gives you the answer you demanded.
Following Jesus even when His answer costs you something.
Not trusting every thought that enters your mind.
Trusting the Christ who entered death itself for you…
Because when your feelings are screaming, your circumstances are confusing, and you cannot distinguish desire from direction, you still have something stronger than an impression.
You have the Word of God.
You have a crucified and risen Savior.
And you can place even your uncertainty into His hands.
Maybe the voice you most desperately need to recognize is not the one telling you what happens next—but the Shepherd who already proved at the cross how far He would go to bring you home.
